utterances.text: Now let us see page SA 40-- actually, it's page 3 in this document. 1D8294, actually. D294. That's it. Let, let me inform you while we're waiting for it, as for these notebooks on -- concerning this council held on the 15th of October, Petko Cancar says, "The president of the constitutional court stated today that the decision taken by the Assembly does not cause any legal effect." Page 3. Let us go to page 3 of this document. Page 3. Perhaps it's different in English. The third page of the document. Page 2 in English. Can we have page 2 in English. Thank you. We see it here, Cancar, in English. It is the last quarter of the page or the third: "[In English] Today the constitutional court stated that the decision adopted by the Assembly did not have any legal effect." Did you see that the president of the constitutional court said that this was an unlawful decision taken by the Assembly, but the SDA continued as if it had been a legally valid decision.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're citing here a statement by an SDS leader about another statement that he alleges was made by the president of the constitutional court. He's not citing a decision of the constitutional court itself. And, in fact, the -- there was a proposal in one of the negotiating sessions during the time of this dead-line that you put on the talks of the 24th, between the 15th and the 24th, to submit the entire issue to the constitutional court. The SDS rejected that suggestion, and on the grounds that they didn't trust the composition of the constitutional court to come up with the decision that they made. So I don't necessarily disbelieve that he said that, but I think that this is not an adequate statement of the fact, claim, that the constitutional basis for the decision was -- was invalid. I think in general this -- to save a lot of time, this is -- this is a meeting at which a lot of different viewpoints were put forward, and they were aired very openly, very democratically, if you will, on the part of the members of the council, and so you can find here a lot of very differing ideas. There weren't sharp disagreements about what to do next. I think there was general agreement on this idea of a seven day or ten day hiatus to allow the negotiations to go forward. I'm not contesting that at all. And then there were some suggestions about intensifying regionalisation. So this is what I see as the first, sort of the beginning of the extended planning process that was set off in the immediate aftermath of the events of the 15th of October, the planning process that you and the SDS went forward with, and it's -- it's a very open discussion of the options that are available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I said I was wondering about the relevance of your line of questioning, in particular how they are impinging upon the indictment. Do not take it for granted that your time for cross-examination will be extended. As you suggested, there are a lot of further issues which are very important and relevant to your case. For example, Variant A or B. Bear that in mind and please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted us to see that the president of the constitutional court had actually made such a statement but that the SDA nevertheless continued with this kind of activity. Thank you. This has already been admitted. Can we now have 00972. That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was yet again unnecessary comment from you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This has been admitted as Exhibit P958, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Donia, that you have referred to this speech of mine that relates to the plebiscite. The Assembly of the Serb people had already been established on the 25th; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 24th, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Possibly. Possibly. Yes, but it was published on the 25th. So we established that to this day the Assembly consists of 83 MPs, and in addition to the SDS, there was the Serb Renewal Movement in this Assembly, then the Reformists, the Socialists -- or, rather, the Communists, and one member who came from the ranks of the Liberals; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I believe there were -- it's four or five delegates. The original Assembly had 11 members of the Reformist Party and 11 members of the Social Democratic Party in the Council of Citizens, and I believe a few of those Serbs who were in those parties joined the Assembly, joined the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that at the time a decision was passed to organise a plebiscite of the Serb people to see whether the Serb people actually supported our policy of remaining in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Dr. Donia -- I'm sure that you are more familiar with this particular field than I am, and that is American history, and that is that President Lincoln started a war against the south because they wanted to change the nature of the American federation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the relevance of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is in the following question:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Dr. Donia, that part of Virginia had refused, refused to join the confederacy and that they stayed with the union, and that is the present-day state of West Virginia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd love to talk about the American civil war forever. I think it's very interesting. But I don't believe that what you have just characterised as a -- changing the state of the federation is an accurate representation of the -- of the condition in the American -- in the American state as of -- in the United States as of 1861.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone. Mr. Karadzic, turn your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you are not disputing that the war started because the south wanted a confederacy? The southern states, rather.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would dispute that. It was a factor but certainly not the only factor in a very complex situation that included issues about admission of new states to the union, the issue of slavery and states' rights, a number of things that I just don't see happening here. Perhaps you do, but I don't see the -- I don't see the riveting parallel that would lead me to conclude what you have, evidently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Virginia was a single state and that West Virginia was created during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when West Virginia was created. Approximately at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I just remind you, the western part of Virginia refused to join the confederacy. They stayed within the union. Do you think that this west part of Virginia was secessionist in relation to the confederacy, or, rather, they had voted for the union and they stayed in the union; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, said I was wondering the relevance of the questions, but you still continue that line of questions, ignoring the advice from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'm sorry. This is a flagrant precedent but let's move on. Can we have page 8 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see this here? "What is important for us is that the plebiscite goes off with dignity and good spirits the way Serbs can do it, like gentlemen," et cetera? And towards -- and further down: "Be on best terms with your Muslim and Croatian neighbours. Just like that, that's no problems for you, no problems for us either. We are just expressing our will. Everything will be fine, no conflict anywhere whatsoever. There can be no shooting. I -- I don't know who gave those weapons to Serbs, but -- oh, go ahead, shoot. Oh, no, you are shooting. You are shooting. That's what I'm saying. You are shooting. See, there's no discipline. This morning at Pale, I said that I would want Serbs to be meek like Muslims or Croats." And then further down it says: "Serbs don't trust a leader until they have weighed him carefully, and then they watch him to see if he would do something wrong or betray them." So I'm talking about the plebiscite. I'm asking that there be no shooting. I'm asking for a good life together with Muslim and Croatian neighbours. The plebiscite is just an expression of one's will, not entering a conflict; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there are about six or seven statements that preceded your question "Right," and I'd have to go back over them one by one to affirm them or deny them. I -- I love this paragraph, because it -- it must have been fun to give that talk. I didn't know any of these people except Professor Koljevic, and I just can't imagine urging this crowd, be sure you don't drink and be monks at your job. It was obvious that you were worried that some sort of unrest might break out and that you were intent on making sure that this happened without incidents as logically you should have, so that the results would be more likely to be accepted as valid by other Bosnian and by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted. Oh, it has already been admitted. Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 5842. This is the Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, number 1. So we started issuing our own Official Gazettes -- has that come up on our screens? Yes, it has. I need the first page. Page 1, please. 7315 are the last digits, whereas the last digits are 7321 here. So six pages on, please. Or, rather, six pages back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that the e-court has only two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what's the second page then? Let's have a look at that. This is the whole of that Official Gazette. So can we put it on the overhead projector, page 1 on the overhead projector, please. It's the decision on the founding of the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that decision was published. Now I'd like us to focus on paragraph III, which says why it was formed in the first place, and what its aims are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the decision, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I'm familiar with the parallel Official Gazette that you formed, I guess believing it to be the equivalent of the legal Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I -- can I ask if this decision was also published in the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we considered the -- that the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not exist, was no longer in existence, because the state was abolished.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you believe that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Constitution, the constitution. Interpreter's correction, the constitution was abolished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So this is, indeed, a parallel document to the official legal gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at item number III: "The Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina shall consider and decide upon all issues which relate to the realisation of the equality of the Serbian people with the other nations and nationalities living in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the protection of the interests of the Serbian people if those interests were to come under threat by decisions of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, does this remind you of what the council of Chambers should have been doing or the council for national equality, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well it reminds me what the Bosnian Serb Assembly was doing which was arrogating unto itself the role of a sole spokesman for the Serb people in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see lower down it says that Serbian deputies would continue the work in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the working bodies to which they were elected, et cetera, et cetera. That's in paragraph 4. Now do you see that the role the Serbian people there is a corrective role against the unconstitutional decisions of the joint Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again it arrogates to the promulgator of this decision, the right or the judgement of what was constitutional and what was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now I have to ask you this: How did Badinter come to the make the decision that Yugoslavia no longer existed? But I don't want to expand the topic. Let me tender this document into evidence first, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D296, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. But I'm not sure you, Doctor, have answered to the question of the accused: How did Badinter come to the -- come to make the decision that Yugoslavia no longer existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour, I have not. The -- what's called the Badinter Commission was, in fact, the Arbitration Commission of the European Community, and it was assigned the task by the European Community ministers of assessing the applications for independence of any of those republics of Yugoslavia that wish to apply for recognition. This body took on this task in December of 1991, deliberated, issued a couple of different statements, the most -- the two most significant of which were a statement of principles whereby they intended to apply the basic principles of human rights and international law to the situation in both the former Yugoslavia -- or the Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union, which was also at that time in turmoil with some of the -- or with the various republics separating from one another, and then subsequently issued a finding citing the various principles and criteria that had been outlined previously based on applications from the various republics. Of the republics -- of the six republics, four ended up applying for recognition. Croatia -- the republics of Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the decision on each of those applications was a little bit different, but in the case of Slovenia and Croatia was an agreement to recognise those two republics on the 15th of January, 1992. I forget what the date was to be for Macedonia, but the provision for Bosnia-Herzegovina was that the will of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina to opt for independence had not been sufficiently established, and, in fact, cited as evidence of the fact that it had not been sufficiently established, the meeting of the Assembly of the Serb people, the Bosnian Serb Assembly, on the 24th of October. And to remedy that prescribed that Bosnia-Herzegovina should hold a referendum on the question of whether the populous sought independence -- sought recognition, I'm sorry, sought recognition as an independent republic at some future time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the order and sequence of events was different? The Badinter Arbitration Commission was supposed to propose a solution to the Yugoslav crisis, what it did was it proposed that Yugoslavia cease to exist.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not at all the case. That's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the sentence that was uttered was "Yugoslavia ceased to exist," that that was the sentence that was remembered?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The memorable sentence was that Yugoslavia was in a process of disillusion. It wasn't that it cease to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Process of disillusion. But a year before that, Gianni De Michelis said Yugoslavia has ceased to exist -- or, rather, that the death of Yugoslavia was proclaimed as a natural phenomenon of Yugoslavia withering and dying away.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that to be the case and I don't have any document in front of me to suggest that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to present the Badinter findings in due course. I didn't think we would need that, but we might. Now, do you agree that it was stated that the republics who wanted to, after the Badinter Commission, that is, that was the conclusion of the ministers of the European Community, that by 21st of December, I think it was, that the republics should tender their request for recognition of independence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tender their request for recognition by the EC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is it also true and correct that before the Badinter decision was made only two republics, Slovenia and Croatia, had put in that request, and they held their referendums; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the requests, I think, did come in -- the formal requests came in subsequent to the Badinter Commission inviting them. There is, of course, a whole history prior to that going back to June 25th, 1991, when Slovenia and Croatia actually declared their independence, the interventions of the EC and negotiations which led to the deferral of the effectiveness of those proclamations for three months until October 18, 1991. So certainly one could say that the -- the process of moving toward independence was very well advanced prior to the Badinter Commission's solicitation of requests. But it did, in fact, invite all republics to respond and, in fact, to comment on its procedures. And Serbia and Montenegro did so liberally, and opined upon both the standards that were to be used and the specific decisions that that the Badinter Commission reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to tender the previous document as a whole, the Official Gazette, Official Gazette number 1. May it be given a number. I'm sure it exists somewhere. It must exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we talking about Exhibit D296? It has been admitted in its entirety. It's admitted, but -- yes, it's admitted. Being marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in the interim, Your Honour, while we're back on the subject, we have been able to locate a translation which hasn't been uploaded in e-court yet, but perhaps we could sort that out at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now may we have 65 ter 225 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, we're now going to move on to the document with Variants A and B, the well-known document that's been exploited so many times. And while we're waiting for that to come up, let me ask you this: Do you remember that the government, on the 20 -- or, rather the 19th of December, I think it was, the BH government, with opposition from the Serb ministers, asked nonetheless that the European Community launch proceedings -- or, rather, called for independence for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. It was the case that both the Presidency and the government, that is the Council of Ministers, appealed in response to the invitation of the European Community appealed for recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a -- as an independent republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that we had three comments and criticisms to make? First of all, that the Assembly should do that, not the government or Presidency; and secondly that neither the government nor the Presidency could reach that decision by out-voting the Serb members because it was an important subject matter which required a consensus.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, your position basically shifted from wanting a two-thirds vote to wanting consensus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we asked for a consensus in the government and Presidency, but a two-thirds majority in the Assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember that the Serb ministers left the government -- or, rather, left the government session and made a public announcement saying that Serb rights had been violated and that of those ministers only one of them was an SDS member?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember that on the 21st of December held an Assembly session, an Assembly of the Serb people, and called for those decision to be withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring now to the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 21st of December. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you will remember that we said that if that wasn't withdrawn by Christmas or whatever that we would set up our own unit in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a little bit more specific than that. I think you -- the SDS or the delegates to the -- what I call Bosnian Serb Assembly voted to make preparations for the proclamation of a separate state, separate Bosnian Serb state and indicated your intent to proclaim that state if the HDZ and the SDA didn't change their behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to draw everybody's attention to the title page of this document. Do you see there, Dr. Donia that, it says that the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Main Board, and that there's no reference number or the usual attributes that attend documents that have been adopted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of our position -- or, rather, what we stated, that we received this document from well-intentioned pensioned officers after they and we proclaimed that their flats should be marked with respect to a tax against their apartments?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of your contention, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you come across a single document stating that this document was discussed and adopted by the organs of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of documentary evidence that it was forwarded to local Municipal Boards by the -- by the Main Board, and this from a variety of different municipalities. I think if your question more narrowly is have I seen a document that is, you know, stamped and signed from the party of the Main Board, the answer's no, I've not. And, in fact, the document internally has a certain inconsistency, because on the front page it says, "Main Board," and the last page it's signed as "Crisis Staff of the Main Board."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have page 2 of the Serbian, and it's still on page 1 in the English, so that we can look at the first paragraph: "Because there is reasonable grounds for suspicion that certain forces are working persistently, thoroughly, and in an organised way to take Bosnia-Herzegovina and then also the Serb people out of Yugoslavia by force, we hereby issue these instructions detailing the common tasks, measures," et cetera. Do you see that? And may we turn to page 2 in the English as well now, please. Thank you. I claim, and we stated this straight away, that this was supplied by that group of well-intentioned officers and many of them were alive in 1941, and that we -- we gave this to people, or, rather, we told people to take note of this and act accordingly should they see fit.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is: Do you agree that once we received this at the Main Board session, that we distributed it without a discussion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't -- I have not seen any documentation on that Main Board session that would lead me to either agree or disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All our documentation stayed behind, because we didn't expect a war. And you know that all our documents were seized. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not all your documents were seized, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what wasn't seized then by the Serbian Democratic Party -- of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. You do. I don't. Clearly there were a lot of things that were not seized because some of them were kept by you and other people in the party over the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May we now turn to page 4279, or, rather, page 5 of this same document to look at item 8. In English it's probably page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it should be the previous page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the next page in Serbian and the previous page in English. And would you look at item 8 in English. And it will come up in the Serbian on page 5. Next page in the Serbian, please. The recommendation made here in point 7 is: "To prevent uncontrolled shipment of deficient products, raw materials, and manufacturing components, step up information -- or, rather, place under control existing commodity reserves," et cetera. And in point 8: "Step up, or, rather, ensure respect for national and other rights of the members of all nations and nationalities and their engagement in the organs of power of authority that the Serbian Assembly will establish in the municipality." Do you agree that this piece of paper is a recommendation for action in a situation of crisis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I am not sure whether you read out the item 8 which is consistent with the English translation we have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It wasn't that. Where it says "Variant B." Before we come to chapter Variant B, that item 8. I think it might be page 4 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we're on page 4. Could you help us locate the passage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it must be page 3. That's it. Paragraph 7, they're telling us to prevent uncontrolled distribution of food and other deficient commodities, stop smuggling and so on, and then point 8 it says: "When taking all these measures [In English] make sure that national and other rights of members of all nations are respected and that they are later engaged in government organs established by the Assembly of Serbian Republic of -- Serbian people of -- in municipality." [Interpretation] Do you agree that this document was a recommendation for action in extreme situations of crisis where there would be no central power and authority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would agree with the first part of that formulation. It certainly is a document that directs activities to be undertaken in a situation of crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this was page 6 of the English, 6 of 10 pages, then I think we need to turn to page 8 of 10. And it's also page 8 of the Serbian. Or maybe it's page 9 of 10 in the English. Probably page 9 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the previous paragraph, Mr. Donia, do we see that the rights of others are to be respected and that they also be included in the organs of power and authority as soon as the situation allows for that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think it said quite that. I think it said after -- again, you're asking me about something that's no longer in front of me, so -- I'm perfectly willing to go back to it, but you've moved on to something else here, so I can't attest to what it -- what it said in the previous section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can we go back to point 8 on page 6 in English. Page 6 in English. So let us see what is envisaged. Can you have a look at it now? "[In English] When taking all these measures," [Interpretation] measures had already been listed, "[In English] Make sure that national and other rights of members of all nations are respected and that they are later engaged in government organs established by the Assembly of Serbian people in the municipality."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think the sequence here is revealing. That is, these measures are to be undertaken first while fully respecting the rights of members of other nations and then later, not specified when or under what conditions they are to be engaged in government organs established by the Assembly of the Serbian people. So it is clear that this is something that will take place at the sufferance of the Assembly of the Serbian people which had been established a month before. Two months before, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, there is a reference here to Municipal Assemblies, Serb Municipal Assemblies; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, the -- and some of those had indeed -- those were to be established under the terms of the instructions. So I erred in assuming that was the central Assembly of Republika Srpska, but, in fact, it is the newly created parallel Assemblies of the Serb peoples that would be created under the terms of the instruction that will then decide when and if others would be engaged in units of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they supposed to decide or is the recommendation that they should join in? [In English] "Make sure they are later engaged."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Make sure that "-- this is in the English and I'd have to go to the Serbian to be absolutely certain, but "make sure that national and other rights are respected and that they are later engaged ..." So, yes, it's a statement of -- at some unspecified later time, the members of these other nations would be engaged in an unspecified way in unspecified government organs established by the Serb municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm noting the time. We will have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just a couple of matters that arose from the last session, Your Honour, if I may. The first is with respect to the document which bore the 65 ter number 1D01362, and we -- that was mentioned at pages 41 and 42 of today's transcript. This document is what -- Dr. Karadzic described this document as a session of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on the 15th of October. It, in fact, appears on the basis of the translation of the heading to have been a meeting between the president and members of the socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency and the socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of president of the government with high officials of the SSNO and the SFRJ armed forces HQ, and we do not have that document in house, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The second item is with respect to 65 ter 05842, which was admitted in full as D296. That has now been up loaded in full in e-court in English and in the original language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you have no objection to admission of it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it's admitted. And taking this opportunity, whether you are in a position to answer questions -- questionnaire provided to the accused some time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That -- we've been looking at those proposed facts in detail and note, Your Honours, that much of those proposed facts are indeed irrelevant on the basis of Your Honour's -- this Chamber's own ruling of 13 April 2010 in regard to the -- from the decision on the Prosecution's motion for admission of the evidence of KDZ172, in particular, paragraph 19 of that decision. There are some matters that may be relevant that we're looking at in more detail, and we'll be able to respond in writing on those, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I ask for the document to be returned, 225? That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In order to get to the war as soon as possible, Mr. Donia, I'm going to try to put questions that are as short as possible. Do you remember that the Serb side had proposed that wherever there was a concentration of one or the other people or nation within a municipality that they actually could establish a municipality of their own?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any formal proposal to that degree. It was certainly inherent in some of the party's programme and policies, but I don't -- couldn't identify a specific document or demand that says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that we had proposed that Sarajevo be reorganised like Brussels? To have ethnic municipalities established, just like municipalities in Brussels are?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my understanding of the way that you ultimately did organise the Serb municipalities in Sarajevo in January/February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you see what is meant by this, namely that they would take part in this life when there is a Serb municipality, meaning that there might be a Croat municipality as well or a Muslim municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't interpret this instruction to be -- to say that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the instruction. I'm just talking about that sentence, namely that they would take part in the political life of the municipality once it is established. Is the reference being made to a Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is. I'm -- again, it's not in front of me here, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know -- I'm sure that you did that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph number 8. The last sentence in paragraph number 8.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- as I said earlier, this clearly establishes that the government organs concerned have to be established by the Assembly of the Serb people. So any such organisations or organs would be created or not by the -- the Assembly of the Serb people, and at some unspecified future time those of other nations might enter into those government organs. It doesn't, for example, say the members of other nations have the right to establish their own organs within a declared Serb municipality. It simply says the government organs established by the Assembly of the Serb people in that municipality will be open at some future time to participation by those of other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in practically all municipalities there were negotiations to the effect that each community would establish its own municipality. In Sanski Most, for instance, in Vlasenica and Bratunac. Actually, in Vlasenica and Bratunac that had already been established. And in Ilidza it had almost been accomplished, too, that is to say to establish a Serbo-Muslim municipality wherever possible?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only situations that I know of like that, and I would be open to knowing of other ones, were those negotiations undertaken essentially at the point of a gun starting in early April 1992, usually with an ultimatum of some sort issued by the SDS just prior to the actual takeover and ethnic cleansing of the municipality concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you cannot put it that way, Mr. Donia. Let's actually finish with this document. Can you find in the document any measure that is offensive -- or, rather, are they all defensive, protective?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Offensive -- you're making the distinction between offence in the sense of advancing and taking something as opposed to defensive which is just to protect what one already has? Is that the distinction you want to make here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes, for instance. However, does it have to do with the defence of the Serb people, or does it have to do with conquests of any kind? Is there anything offensive in this paper?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is offensive to me, and in various ways it specifies that the representatives of the Serb Democratic Party or other organs established by them take from the existing institutions of the municipality control over raw materials, commodities, and various procedures. They essentially seize parts or functions, take over functions that would have been previously exercised by the government of the municipality. Number 6: "Take over the staff, buildings and equipment of security services centres and place them at the disposal of the newly established organs ... " That's seizure. That's a seizure of power. It's an offensive act not a defensive preservation of the -- what you're characterising here as the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in these negotiations on the establishment of two or more municipalities in previously existing municipalities it had been envisaged for the other side to do the same thing, to establish their own police station and their own organs? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I'm not aware of any -- I'm not aware of any negotiations of that character beforehand. Would I think it likely that some did and some were undertaken, but I don't really know of any, so I can't really answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember when one says the Serb municipality of Sanski Most, it means that there is also a Muslim municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's your characterisation of it. Anything that's not Serb is automatically part of a different nation's property, and you don't seem to recognise that there was something called the common life that was shared by various -- all -- all peoples or peoples in that particular municipality, and that presupposition is critical to your argument about the right of the Serb people or the right of the SDS in the name of the Serb people to seize these -- these assets. You presuppose that the only way this can be dealt with is through division or separation of economic resources, of means of production, of goods and services, of governmental institutions. It goes right to your assumption that all possession must be ethnic in character and that you have the right to act on behalf of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've been waiting for the interpretation. D85, D85 temporarily. That has already been admitted. D85. English page 4, the last paragraph. You will see what kind of recommendation this was and with cases it actually referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D85. That is a document that has already been admitted. Page 4, the last paragraph in the English version. In Serbian it's page 3. In English it's page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here it is in English: "[In English] On the basis of the discussion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it page 4?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, page 4, the last paragraph. And in Serbian, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "On the basis of the discussion, the president formulated two amendments to the recommendation. "It is recommended that the SDS, Serbian Democratic Party deputies clubs in the municipality Assemblies in B and H where decisions against Serbian interests are imposed through out-voting ..." [Interpretation] So where decisions are detrimental or were detrimental because they were imposed through out-voting. "[In English] The decision of the Serb Democratic Party deputies clubs to transform themselves into Assemblies of Serbian people in ..." [Interpretation] Could we have the next page now, please: "[In English] Municipality," I suppose. [Interpretation] The next page, please: "[In English] In B and H shall be verified by the Assembly of the Serbian people ..." [Interpretation] Mr. Donia, the recommendation for establishing new municipalities was amended by either myself or Krajisnik, I'm not sure who it was. Namely that this should be done only in municipalities where decisions are being imposed on the Serb people by way of out-voting, decisions that are detrimental to the Serb people. And in the Municipal Assembly or parliament then the MPs would form a separate municipality and Assembly and then they would form their communities of municipalities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- this is this very, I think, pivotal third session at which the proposal initially made by Mr. Krajisnik and endorsed by you was to -- language to the effect that it was required that the SDS delegates in most municipalities inhabited by Serbs form these separate Serb associations or municipalities, Assemblies, if you will. And that resolution passed with one dissenting vote, after which there was an extensive discussion by various delegates in which you participated and Mr. Krajisnik participated in which it became clear that many delegates felt this was an ill-advised measure to take in some municipalities, because it would destroy the co-operation, such as it was then, under the terms of the inter-party agreements and make -- convey the impression that the SDS would invite formation of separate municipalities by -- by other national groups, and it was after this extensive discussion that the amendments came forth, and I also don't remember exactly who proposed these, but it was eventually passed owing to the objections of these various delegates in such a way that it was made voluntary. And, in fact, the -- I think the cover sheet that was to be distributed to the municipalities was to specify that it would be a voluntary action. And the judgement in this situation, the judgement of whether the interests of the Serbian people had been violated, whether there was out-voting, would, of course, rest in the hands of the local SDS or even the republic SDS officials, and then on that basis they would decide whether to proceed and form a Serbian Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you agree that we should look at the results, the products of every Assembly, the documents that are adopted rather than the discussion that take place while the Assembly is in session? Don't you see that this decision or recommendation was improved by way of these amendments and that it pertained to those municipalities where solutions were imposed by way of out-voting the Serb delegates? This is a good example showing that one should look at decisions reached by Assemblies rather than the debates that take place beforehand. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially. I think one should look at the decisions that were preached at various Assembly sessions. I think they tell a very interesting but incomplete story of the direction in which the party policy was moving. I think one also should look at the debates, and, in fact, that's the source of the richness of these transcripts, and I think they're going to be used because of their richness by you, and as well they are rich in terms of the kind of things that I investigate. So I don't agree that we should just look at decisions. I would think we should look at the way in which decisions were reached and also what -- what happened afterwards, and I think that your own dissatisfaction with the decisions reached at this -- the voluntary nature of these things is a direct source of the nature of the document, the A/B document that we've been looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where was it that you found that I was dissatisfied with this decision? Let not waste any time. Just indicate it to us. Where is this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't, sitting here, go through the whole Assembly session. I think your -- your dissatisfaction with it was -- was expressed during the course of the debate about it when you defended the notion that it was important to establish these, and in your subsequent conversation with Mr. Krajisnik that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has already been admitted, but now could I have a new document, 1D01405. 010415. It hasn't been translated. It is hand written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope that you will be able to read this in Cyrillic. This is an agreement between the two peoples, the SDA and the SDS. I mean, they represent the two peoples. That's what I'm saying. On the basis of a principled agreement between the representatives of the SDA and the SDS and the representatives of the two municipalities on the partition of the municipality of Bratunac into two Assemblies, the Serb and the Muslim Assembly, reached on the 5th of April, 1992. The representatives of the two parties in power, that is to say the SDA and the SDS, met up on the 8th of April, 1992, and reached --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. 65 ter 00739, with the translation available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then further on before we get it, it says that: "The representatives of both peoples accepted reality, that the partition of the municipalities was inevitable and could be carried out in a peaceful and democratic way." Then number 2: "The establishment of a Serbian public security station in that Bratunac and the partition of the existing public security station is the first step in that direction. "3. We should also try to explain these agreements. "5. The people who have moved out of our areas should be invited back and the schools should re-open. "7. The relocation and demobilisation of military and other armed formations in the area of municipalities should begin immediately. "9. To make it impossible for any kind of paramilitary and military formations to come to this area and that both peoples should resist aggression if they feel --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "11. To involve equal numbers of Serb and Muslim policemen, that they should be engaged. "12. That both public security stations should guarantee peace and safety to the citizens. "13. Plans and tasks of both chiefs should be co-ordinated and joint on-site investigations should be conducted. "14." -- or, "15. Disputes and problems should be resolved in a peaceful and democratic way." And my question is: Do you see, Mr. Donia, that this is one -- that this is a municipality which -- or one of the municipalities which, at the beginning of the war, endeavoured to reorganise one joint municipality in two municipalities, and this happened in Vlasenica so those two agreements were reached; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to see the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't have them here, but we have statement by Rabija Subic. Do you know who she was, Rabija Subic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was an extreme nationalist spokesperson for pretty much everything you believed in. And spoke on a number of occasions to the Bosnian Serb Assembly. She was, I think, the head of a small party which was called the Serbian Socialist Party or something like that. Yugoslav Socialist Party in Bosnia. This document bears all the earmarks of an agreement dictated by one side. It is in Cyrillic, which would only be used by a Serb, at a fraught time in this municipality and cannot possibly have been agreed to on a voluntary basis by the people that you said agreed to it. I think it's a good example of what I just cited, these last-minute talks held at the point of a gun, usually with an ultimatum attached as the SDS was preparing to take -- assume full power in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you think that 30 per cent Serbs can force 70 per cent Muslims in Bratunac to do this job?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking Bratunac; right? Not Vlasenica. I think somebody mentioned Vlasenica earlier. They had the backing of the JNA. They had paramilitaries available to them. It was, as I say, at the point of a gun, and I think subsequent events in Bratunac in the period after this supposed agreement bear that out, and I don't -- it's not my -- my role to go into what those were, but I think it also makes all the more empty and all the more just -- it makes it into a mere gesture these statements about the rights of other peoples in the course of the Serb seizure of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I am deeply dissatisfied with the breath of your explanations. Do you know that throughout Bosnia there was this process of agreement and negotiating between Muslims and Serbs to reorganise the municipalities into two municipalities, ethnic ones? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I put this to you, I put it to you that what was envisaged was that in that kind of Serb municipality there would also be Muslims and that they would be included into the political life of the Serb municipality. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that a similar agreement was reached at -- well, in Vlasenica first and then at Ilidza later on, and that the process of negotiation had progressed in Sanski Most, Kljujic, and other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you must have known that, Mr. Donia, because they're facts, and we'll show that. We'll show that they're facts. And if you don't know about them then you didn't do your job.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd love to see the documents that -- that show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You'll see them. You'll see proof and evidence, but I'd like to tender this document first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D297, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we briefly go back to 65 ter 225 to finish our discussions on that document and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that whoever wrote this, the document was distributed on the 19th of December, 1991, after the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had asked for recognition of independence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you see anywhere there that any kind of aggressive or offensive action is anticipated vis-a-vis others outside the realm of the protection of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, in expressing its intent to take over the functions and resources of the existing municipalities, yes, it does express a hostile intent towards the property and -- of others and the functions being exercised by others in the municipality, and those others would necessarily have involved those members of other peoples and probably some Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you're going back to the thesis that there wasn't a plan and intention and programme and platform and the realisation on the formation of Serb municipalities, because we're dealing with Serb resources in those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you kind of define Serb resources the way you chose to. You certainly define Serb land in a way that was convenient to justify the seizure of land and expansion of authority at the municipal level right from about this time into really at least the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, this seems to be a criticism rather than an answer. Based on international pact on human rights, who do resources belong to, the people that live there or to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'd have to look at the specific provision you have in mind to -- to give you an answer to that. I wouldn't say it belongs to somebody else, but exactly how it's formulated I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you must have known that. If you hold it against us that we said that the Serb power and authority and the Serb portion of the municipalities would manage its resources, then you must know that this is net based on the international pact and covenant on human rights. It is an important article, resources and natural wealth belong to the nation living on the land. That's what it says in the international covenant. Now, can you give another example which this group of officers of an offensive action, that this group of officers envisaged? And please understand that we're talking about the Serb part of each municipality.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not too sure what you mean by "Serb part of each municipality." The municipality was an administrative unit that didn't distinguish between people on the basis of their ethnicity and didn't distinguish between pieces of land on the basis of the ethnicity of who owned it. So that remains to me to be clarified before I could really answer that part of your question. We can go through the document if you wish, and I can point out those passages which, to me, indicate an aggressive or intent to seize or to -- to contemplate or prepare for the seizure of commonly held assets. I would be glad to do that. I see only, you know, the first page in front of me here, which is really the title page and the preamble which, in my mind, is the only thing that probably wasn't written by military officers, the rest of it being very military in its -- in its structure and composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we turn to the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Edgerton, do you have the hard copy of this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not immediately but shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be handed over to -- to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, where did you see state property at that point in time? Did state property exist at all at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did exist, and so did -- so did social property. And as -- we talked about this last week, probably about 53 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina made up socially-owned land, and so private property, privately held land, was, in fact, a minority of the total territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as of sometime in the very late 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. While we're waiting for that document to come up, may we -- or, rather, may we now have another document on our screens, 1D1170. May we have that called up. And let's have a look, Mr. Donia, what is going on parallelly to the Serb actions, what the other side is doing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, 107 is the correct number. 1D107. 1D107.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian version we see that it is a decision on promoting to the rank of brigadier-general of the army of -- the Republic of Bosnia [indiscernible] for Sefer Halilovic, signed by Alija Izetbegovic; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't -- I see a B/C/S document here dated 26 April 1994 and an English translation dated 8 April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1994, is his statement, his request. The decision came after that, on the 26th of April. But this is on the 8th of April, 1994. Sefer Halilovic is requesting that his status be resolved. That's the subject of this document: "[In English] Request to resolve status."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karadzic. In the B/C/S, Alija Izetbegovic signed the document, but in the English document we only see the name of Sefer Halilovic. So I take it those two are different documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could assist, Your Honour. If we go to page 2 in the B/C/S version, I think you'll see the same content in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 2 of the Serbian. The first page is Izetbegovic's title -- decision pertaining to Halilovic's request, and the right-hand side is Halilovic's request two weeks before the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you see in paragraph 1: "[In English] As an active serviceman." [Interpretation] "As an active serviceman of the former JNA, Yugoslav People's Army, seeing what was going to happen I left that army, and in September 1991, applied myself with total commitment to the function of organising preparations for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the aggression I anticipated." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the next paragraph after the word "Corps": "[In English] Corps I drew up a proposal. [Interpretation] I drew up a proposal for organising the Patriotic League for the Sarajevo region and the regional staff of the Patriotic League and a plan of defence for the Sarajevo region. When I met President Alija Izetbegovic in Hrasnica, when I informed him of what had been done up until then and proposed a way of organising the Muslim people and other citizens of the republic," et cetera, et cetera, "and a strategy," et cetera. And the last paragraph in Serbian, probably English too, it reads: "After that," that's right: "After that, I set out to realise the plan that had been accepted in organising the Main Staff of the Patriotic League of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 9 regional military staffs, 19 municipal military staffs of the Patriotic League, and a large number of manoeuvre area and logistical units." Now, do you know what in the meantime was being done by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meantime of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, at the same time. You know, what the Serbs were doing at the time: Exclusively political moves they were making. Now, did you know what the other side was doing and forcing the Serbs to react and take political steps? They were provoking the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't share the premise of your question that the Serbs at that time were only doing political moves. I think that the SDS was busy arming its -- its people and becoming essentially a paramilitary unto itself, and all sorts of things were going on to make sure that the SDS had the co-operation and support of the JNA in pursuing whatever course it might choose to take after the fall of 1991. This account squares very well with my own understanding of the growth of the Patriotic League, which was a really skeletal organisation until at least this September 1991 date when the war in Croatia really alienated a lot of the non-Serb officers of the JNA and caused them to leave the JNA and join various other bodies that were organising at the time. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm not interested in your interpretation of this. I'm just interested in facts. Do you want to say that in September 1991, the Serbian Democratic Party was in favour of the disintegration of Yugoslavia and that it -- and that it -- the JNA served it apart from the fact that the SDS supported the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not make that statement and don't believe that that was the case. I think the -- the coming together of the SDS and the JNA or what really proved to be a very close working alliance was just getting started in the early couple of weeks of -- of September 1991, and they grew closer but somewhat erratically in the months after that. There clearly were some efforts on the part of the JNA to distribute arms to members of the SDS prior to that, but in terms of the kind of top-level co-operative relationship that -- that started about this same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to the question of the JNA. What I'm asking you now is this: You noticed and said yourself that the Serbian Democratic Party claimed that all its moves were in response to the moves made by the other side; right? Like moves on a chessboard.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. I just referenced your statement, and you made it, I think, twice later in the war to the effect that you basically timed your actions to wait for a measure taken by Mr. Izetbegovic before taking that action. I would be glad to look at those specific quotes that I referenced if you'd like. I don't know exactly the number in my report, but that's what I referenced. That's what I believed to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you knew of our position. Were you aware of our position that our moves were provoked by the moves and steps taken by the other side? I asked you that on day one, and you said, Yes. And I asked you why you hadn't studied the moves of the other side, and now I'm putting one of these other moves to you. You thought that we didn't know what Halilovic was doing; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought -- I'm sorry. I thought that you didn't know what Halilovic was doing? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The interpretation wasn't the right one there. Let me put it in simpler terms. Mr. Donia, you said -- you agreed that the Patriotic League was founded on the 31st of March, 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That the committee for the protection of the Muslim peoples had already been constituted and -- with some 500 members and held a meeting in June 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: June 10th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that in September 1991, the Crisis Staff was established in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've written of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I'm putting it to you that Halilovic, Sefer Halilovic left the JNA and already as in -- already in September of 1991 had -- that 98 municipalities had military staffs, 9 regional staffs, 98 municipal staffs, and a large number of manoeuvre logistical units and units in the rear. Was that also a SDA activity then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it a SDA -- no, it was a Patriotic League activity, recognising that the Patriotic League was formed and certainly operated under the general guidance of the -- of the SDA. I don't think he says here that there were 98 municipal military staffs in September. I think he says that he began realising that plan in September, which again would be pretty much according to my understanding of it, this, if you will, embryonic organisation, didn't really take form until September when the war in Croatia began to heat up substantially. And it really wasn't until probably the first of the year that you could speak of a significant force, first of 1992, in a wide variety of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you come across a document confirming that part of the Patriotic League, a part of the leadership of the Patriotic League asked to go to war straight away against Yugoslavia in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll be showing the document in due course. Mr. Donia, up until the beginning of the war -- their document, the SDA documents. It says, up to the beginning of the war, they had military staffs in 103 municipalities. But let's stay with the 98 municipalities. In those 98 municipalities, were there any Serbs living there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were 98, there certainly were Serbs living in some of those municipalities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In most of these municipalities, in fact; right? Except for Cazin and Velika Kladusa; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, at least 90 per cent of the municipalities. Well, the Serbs watched what Halilovic was doing, organising a secret army, assisted by the Muslim section of MUP, and you considered that the Serbs steps were not conditioned and provoked by this unlawful and illegal and dangerous steps taken by the Party of Democratic Action; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't share your characterisation of it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you think that this wasn't dangerous, that it wasn't dangerous to be building up an army is? Who was this army supposed to fight against in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's two questions there. It -- it could have been dangerous, indeed. It was actually the -- it was -- it was not a huge secret. It was a -- something the -- the meeting of June 10th was well covered in the press. Everybody knew about this defence council for the protection of the Muslim peoples, and this specific preparations and arming certainly did go on outside of, let's say, the public -- public eye, but the general movement was -- was well known at the time, and it's well known that you were and the SDS were keeping very careful surveillance of these activities, pretty much knew exactly what was going on. In fact, maintained a very active network of informants and people in these various municipalities and at the republic level who -- who were informing you about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, do you know when it was that we -- well, you saw the letter that we showed earlier on. When did we send this demand for events to be monitored and reported on? That was also the end of September 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at this time the Serbs still did not have any Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what Crisis Staffs did the Serbs have at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me if I agreed that they didn't have any, and I can't agree that they didn't because I've answered your question several times now that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know. Right. So how can you confirm that the SDS itself became a paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the various arming activities that took place in the -- starting about May of 1991, put hands in the very -- or arms in the hands of various local SDS committees. There's a rich gathering of documentation that attests to that, including meetings that members of the SDS had with the officials of the government in Belgrade, a letter from a colonel in the JNA. In fact, the very colonel who was with Mr. Milan Martic when he was detained on the 8th of September, 1991, discussing the distribution of arms in Bosnia. I consider that very well established. And the recipients of those arms were SDS members and SDS local units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have no proof of that, Mr. Donia. But let me ask you something: Do you know of the doctrine and law -- actually, the doctrine is the armed people, and the law has to do with the armed people and all national defence. Do you know of that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you speaking of People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. There was a poor translation, so I just wanted to clarify that. Yes, I do know of the -- let's say theory or doctrine of People's Defence and know that there was a rather elaborate code of laws about the People's Defence, that it was in existence in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know that reservists would always and invariably take their equipment and uniforms home? They would take them out for exercises, training, and bring them back home.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think some of them. I don't think they brought their bazookas home and didn't take their tanks home, but at least in the realm of small arms I think that was a common practice for everybody who was in the People's Defence force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now I'm going to put something to you. The Serb Democratic Party, all the way up until the end while there was peace, supported the JNA and sent reservists on the ready to respond as soon as they were called up by the JNA. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think all three parts of your proposition are the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please, to see what the scope of the further activities of Mr. Sefer Halilovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that these were secret activities of his, that he had concealed them from the army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't had a chance to read the document, and I can't answer the question until I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this part: "From the beginning of December 1991 up until the end of March 1992, five or six times I stayed in all regional municipal staffs of the Patriotic League and in several units of the Patriotic League throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, constantly travelling with false papers, other people's papers, lest I be discovered." Did you see he did that secretly and with false documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the suggestion in this document, yes. I'm just remembering that he was looking for a promotion here and certainly wanted to optimise his own achievements in order to get that promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You think that he could have deceived Izetbegovic? You think that he could have said this without actually having done it? You don't think that Izetbegovic would have known?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Not if the -- what's doing here is just a bit of exaggeration and not -- not making it up. And I -- clearly he's not making it up out of whole cloth, but I wouldn't -- having been a party myself to some efforts to gain promotions for myself and other people in a military organisation, a little exaggeration isn't -- isn't out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Even with exaggerations this, nevertheless, did cause fear among the Serb people. Your answer is going to be "not necessarily."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you ask me a question, I'll try and come up with an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it your understanding that that vast activity, even if there was a bit of exaggeration involved, did lead to fear amongst the Serbs in these 98 municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it could have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you have a somewhat different view of Variant A and Variant B now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serbs were not supposed to take any measures of caution and defence and protection? No?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the A/B document really outlines a series of offensive aggressive actions to seize power and resources in the municipalities, and the defensive component is -- is certainly there, but probably not a -- an appropriate response to what we're looking at here.
